strengths: The paper is well written and clearly motivated, connecting spatial non-uniformity of cross-attention on aesthetic descriptors with temporal redundancy during denoising.

A unified and unusually rigorous evaluation protocol is used (10k Pick-a-Pic prompts, 3 fixed seeds, paired comparisons, end-to-end latency including CFG and VAE decoding), which is better than much of the acceleration literature.

Extensive ablations are provided: component-wise SkipSparse analysis (Table 7), token-weighting strategies (Table 8), sensitivity to skip_ratio and mask_step (Tables 9-10), runtime decomposition (Table 11), and anchor coverage statistics (Tables 12-13).

The spatially adaptive attention design (focus queries with global keys/values, cached background FFN activations) and the spatially varying CFG are sensible engineering, and limitations (architecture dependence, aggressive-sparsity degradation) are honestly discussed.
Experiments span three DiT backbones with multiple training-free baselines (TeaCache, TaylorSeer, RAS, Delta-DiT, FORA, SDiT).
weaknesses: The headline claim - that acceleration simultaneously improves aesthetic quality - rests entirely on automatic preference proxies (ImageReward, HPSv2, LAION Aesthetic) with no human evaluation. These metrics are plausibly gamed by the spatial CFG mechanism (Eq. 11 raises guidance on focus regions), so the improvement may reflect guidance-scale tuning toward the reward models rather than genuinely better denoising. A human study or an ablation of AccelAes with uniform CFG is needed to disentangle this confound.

The core aesthetic-aware contribution (AesMask + spatial SkipSparse) is only fully operational on one of three backbones. On SD3-Medium, spatial CFG is disabled (App. C.5), and on FLUX.1-dev the spatial path is not supported at all, reducing AccelAes essentially to the StepCache component. On FLUX it is also slower (1.73x) than TeaCache (2.14x) and TaylorSeer (2.12x), weakening the claimed 'consistent' advantage; the aesthetic story is effectively validated only on Lumina-Next.

The temporal component (StepCache, linear extrapolation of cached predictions with periodic refresh) is close to existing forecasting/caching methods (FORA, TaylorSeer, TeaCache), so the novelty of the framework is largely in the aesthetics-driven mask and guidance - the component that generalizes least across backbones.

The method depends on a hand-crafted 34-word English anchor vocabulary with a 0.60 CLIP similarity threshold; 35-55% of prompts fall back to uniform cross-attention weighting. The evaluation prompts are biased toward this vocabulary (65.48% trigger rate on the eval set vs 44.9% on the full Pick-a-Pic pool), so measured gains may not transfer to general prompts, non-English prompts, or prompts without explicit aesthetic adjectives.

Comparisons are at mismatched operating points: baselines use official/default settings while AccelAes picks its own Delta, warmup, and skip ratio (tuned on the same metrics reported in the tables), which complicates fair speed-quality ranking; several baseline gains (CLIP, HPS) are small and no variance or significance is reported.
Edge Density is presented as a quality proxy, but it is a weak and arguably misleading metric (higher edge density is not inherently better; TaylorSeer has the best Edge on Lumina).

Ablation evidence for the aesthetic prior is thin in absolute terms: at matched 2.11x speedup, removing AesMask changes ImageReward from 0.822 to 0.841 (0.019), and the spatial path alone gives 1.42x with modest quality gain - the majority of the speedup and part of the quality gain come from the generic temporal cache.
The code link in the abstract is empty ('Code is available at .'), and reproducibility details such as how many of the six metrics were used for hyperparameter selection are not stated.

strengths: The paper is well organized and clearly written: the motivation (spatial non-uniformity tied to aesthetic descriptors) is articulated, the AesMask/SkipSparse/StepCache pipeline is described at a level of detail sufficient to understand and largely re-implement, and hyperparameters, anchor vocabulary, and hardware are reported in the appendix.

The empirical evaluation is broad and fairly rigorous for this area: three DiT backbones (Lumina-Next, SD3-Medium, FLUX.1-dev), a unified protocol over 10k prompts with paired seeds, comparisons against five representative training-free acceleration baselines, and thorough ablations (StepCache-only vs. spatial-only vs. full, token-weighting strategies, skip_ratio, mask_step, runtime decomposition, anchor trigger-rate analysis).

The claim that temporal reuse (StepCache) alone reduces preference metrics while spatial allocation recovers them is supported by the ablation (Table 7, Fig. 5), and the runtime decomposition (Table 11) honestly reports that combined savings are sub-additive.
Limitations are meaningfully discussed (architecture dependence, fragility under aggressive sparsity), and the paper is transparent that FLUX reduces mostly to temporal reuse.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The three components are largely recombinations of established ideas: linear-extrapolation step caching is essentially TaylorSeer-style forecasting, sparse attention with aesthetic-region queries and global K/V resembles ∆-DiT/RAS/SDiT, and the semantic-region-prior idea for budgeting already exists in RAS and SDiT. The genuinely new element is the CLIP-anchor-based 'aesthetic' token weighting, which is a hand-crafted heuristic (a fixed 34-word English vocabulary) rather than a principled signal; no evidence is given that this prior outperforms a learned or generic saliency prior at matched budgets.

The headline claim — that the accelerated method beats the dense baseline (+11.9% ImageReward at 2.11× speedup) — is confounded. Spatial CFG (Eq. 11) raises effective guidance on focus regions, which changes the output distribution and is a known lever for preference metrics. The paper never runs the crucial control: a dense model with equivalent region-weighted guidance. Without it, quality gains cannot be attributed to 'smarter compute allocation' and the acceleration framing is misleading; the ablation shows spatial-only already lifts IR to 0.818 at only 1.42× speedup, which is consistent with a guidance effect rather than redundancy reduction.

No human evaluation, despite the entire contribution being framed around aesthetics and human preference. All quality evidence is from proxy metrics (IR, HPS, LAION Aesthetic, CLIP), and Edge Density is a weak sharpness proxy that a stronger CFG can inflate. Several reported metric gains are small (e.g., CLIP 0.2640 vs 0.2531; HPS +0.003) with no variance or significance testing over the 10k-prompt set.

Baseline fairness is uneven. On FLUX, AccelAes (1.73×) is substantially slower than TeaCache (2.14×) and TaylorSeer (2.12×), and TaylorSeer attains near-identical IR/CLIP/HPS; the claim of a 'better speed–quality trade-off' on that backbone is not clearly supported by the reported numbers.

Robustness and coverage of the aesthetic prior are under-examined. The anchor vocabulary is English-only and hand-curated; the fallback mode (uniform attention weighting) is active for ~35% of Pick-a-Pic prompts, but behavior and quality in that regime are not analyzed. Sensitivity to anchor-list design (category ablations, alternative vocabularies, multilingual prompts) is missing.

The one-shot mask at step 5 sits uneasily with the paper's own observation that aesthetic regions exhibit 'larger temporal variation'; a fixed early mask may mis-localize as content emerges, and the reported sensitivity analysis is aggregate and does not address failure cases where salient regions shift.

Reproducibility is weakened by an incomplete artifact: the abstract states 'Code is available at .' with an empty link. Also, a real-person prompt appears in Fig. 1 without any discussion of person-specific generation risks; the paper has no broader-impact discussion despite concerns pertinent to aesthetics-guided guidance amplification.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated observation: spatial non-uniformity of cross-attention w.r.t. aesthetic descriptors is an interesting signal for compute allocation, and the paper connects it coherently to spatially varying CFG and sparse attention/FFN updates.

Comprehensive and mostly well-executed empirical study: three DiT backbones (Lumina-Next-T2I, SD3-Medium, FLUX.1-dev), a unified protocol (10k Pick-a-Pic prompts, 3 fixed seeds, 30k images per configuration), and comparisons against several recent training-free acceleration baselines (Δ-DiT, FORA, RAS, SDiT, TeaCache, TaylorSeer).

Ablations are substantive rather than token: component-wise decomposition (Table 7, Table 11), AesMask weighting-strategy comparison (Table 8), sensitivity to skip_ratio and mask_step (Tables 9-10), anchor coverage statistics (Tables 12-13), and a candid explanation of why spatial CFG is disabled on SD3 (C.5).

The method is genuinely training-free, plug-in style, and the paper is generally well written with clear notation and reproducibility-oriented details in the appendix (anchor vocabulary, hardware, precision settings).
weaknesses: The core 'aesthetics-aware' contribution is validated on essentially one backbone. On SD3-Medium and FLUX.1-dev the spatial SkipSparse path is disabled or not applicable (A.3), so results there reduce to a linear-extrapolation step cache that closely resembles FORA [37]; the paper does not clearly delineate its novelty relative to FORA-style linear forecasting. On FLUX, both TeaCache (2.14×) and TaylorSeer (2.12×) are faster than AccelAes (1.73×), so the headline contribution rests largely on Lumina-Next.

Quality claims rely entirely on automatic proxy metrics (ImageReward, HPSv2, LAION Aesthetic, CLIP). Since the method explicitly strengthens guidance and computation in regions tied to reward-correlated aesthetic tokens, gains on these reward models may partially reflect optimizing toward the proxies rather than genuine perceptual improvement. No human evaluation or user study is provided to substantiate the central claim of 'improved aesthetics,' which is a significant evidentiary gap for the paper's positioning.

Evidence of possible evaluation-set tuning: hyperparameters (mask_step=5, skip_ratio=0.50, Δ=2, warmup, anchor threshold 0.60) are selected using the same 10k Pick-a-Pic evaluation set used for the main results, without a held-out validation split. This weakens the credibility of reported gains.

Some results appear weak or anomalous for baselines (e.g., FORA at 0.99× speedup on SD3, i.e., no speedup at all), raising concerns about the fairness or fidelity of baseline reproductions; a matched-speedup re-tuning of baselines is not systematically reported.

The spatial path contributes most of the quality gain but comparatively little of the speedup (29.5% standalone saving, and speedup is essentially unchanged across skip_ratio values in Table 9 because temporal caching dominates latency). This slightly undercuts the headline framing that the aesthetic-aware mechanism drives the acceleration.

Minor presentation issues: the code URL in the abstract is empty ('Code is available at .'), some references appear with unusual/future venue years (SDiT arXiv:2601, ICLR 2026, KSII 2026), and Fig. 4/5 contain garbled or hard-to-read embedded text, which hurts clarity.

Framing slightly overstates: the abstract headline (2.11× speedup, +11.9% ImageReward) is from the one backbone where the full method is active; a more honest headline acknowledging the reduced configuration on SD3/FLUX would better match the evidence.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated observation: cross-attention from aesthetic descriptor tokens concentrates on perceptually important regions whose trajectories vary more over timesteps, and this coupling of spatial and temporal non-uniformity is used to guide both compute allocation and caching.

Extensive evaluation: three representative DiT backbones, a large unified protocol (10k prompts, 3 seeds, 30k images per configuration), multiple preference/aesthetic metrics, a blind human preference study with significance testing, prompt/scene robustness checks, hyperparameter sensitivity, runtime decomposition, and an honest failure-case analysis with mitigation (Appendix E).
The method is training-free with small measured overhead (AesMask + Spatial-CFG add ~0.18s, 1.4% of dense latency), and compatibility with a distilled 4-step model (FLUX.1-schnell) is demonstrated.

Thorough ablations (Table 8, Table 9, Tables 10-12) that decompose the contribution of StepCache, spatial sparsification, and AesMask weighting, plus implementation details sufficient for reproducibility (anchor vocabulary, hyperparameters, hardware).
weaknesses: Limited novelty and generalization of the core aesthetic-aware mechanism: the full spatial SkipSparse path works only on Lumina-Next. On SD3-Medium, spatially varying CFG is disabled (Appendix C.5), and on FLUX.1-dev the spatial path is unavailable entirely, so AccelAes there is essentially a linear step-cache; on FLUX it is also slower than TeaCache (1.73x vs 2.14x) and TaylorSeer (2.12x). The claimed transfer of the aesthetics-driven idea to multiple backbones is therefore only partially supported.

The headline speedup is largely attributable to temporal caching rather than the aesthetic component: the standalone StepCache already yields 1.57x, and Table 10 shows speedup stays ~2.11x across skip_ratio 0.30-0.70, indicating the spatial path barely affects latency; its benefit is almost entirely on quality metrics, partly via Spatial-CFG which changes the guidance itself rather than accelerating it.

That an accelerated method consistently beats the dense baseline on ImageReward/CLIP/HPS/Aesthetic (Table 1) is surprising and not fully explained; the effect plausibly comes from stronger guidance on focus regions acting as a regularizer, which conflates acceleration with guidance tuning and raises questions about whether 'acceleration with quality gain' is the right framing.

AesMask relies on a hand-crafted 34-word anchor vocabulary matched via CLIP cosine similarity - a fairly brittle heuristic; anchor-hit coverage is only ~45% of Pick-a-Pic prompts (Table 19), and behavior on prompts outside the vocabulary is only partially characterized. Comparison to learned saliency or entropy-based region priors is not provided.

Comparison coverage is uneven across backbones: RAS and SDiT appear only on Lumina-Next; SD3/FLUX comparisons are limited to caching-based baselines, making cross-backbone claims of superiority over region-adaptive methods hard to verify.

Some technical aspects are thin: Eq. 13 is a first-order linear extrapolation (essentially TaylorSeer order-1), yet the paper reports better stability than TaylorSeer without a principled analysis; the human study is small (15 annotators, 60 pairs); Edge Density as a quality proxy is weakly justified.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant and practical problem (training-free acceleration of Diffusion Transformers) and articulates a clear motivation: computation allocation should follow spatially non-uniform perceptual importance rather than uniform skipping.

Experimental infrastructure is thorough: a unified protocol (10k prompts, fixed seeds, paired comparisons) across three DiT backbones, runtime decomposition, hyperparameter sensitivity analyses, a blind human preference study, prompt-robustness checks, and failure-case analysis with mitigation rules. The supplementary addresses many standard reviewer concerns.

The ablations (Fig. 5, Tables 8-12) are informative, showing that the spatial allocation path and temporal caching are complementary, and that StepCache alone slightly degrades ImageReward while the spatial path improves it.
The authors are candid about limitations: FLUX.1-dev effectively only uses the temporal path, Spatial-CFG is disabled on SD3, and static masks can fail on non-centric prompts.
Writing and structure are generally clear, and the method is training-free and conceptually simple to implement.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is largely a combination of existing ingredients — region-adaptive spatial computation (RAS, SDiT), temporal caching/extrapolation (FORA, TeaCache, TaylorSeer), and spatially varying CFG ([39]). AesMask adds a CLIP-anchor-based token selection on top of standard cross-attention aggregation. The technical core (Eqs. 7-13) is straightforward, and the linear extrapolation cache is very close to prior work.

The headline claim of simultaneously improving preference metrics while removing ~50% of compute is suspicious and likely driven by Spatial-CFG: stronger guidance on focus tokens (gaes >= gbg >= 1) is an aesthetic-enhancement intervention, not a consequence of acceleration. The fair comparison would be a dense baseline with matched or higher guidance; without that, the claimed quality gains over the dense baseline are confounded.

Potential metric circularity: the method keys on aesthetic descriptors in prompts, and its gains are measured largely by preference/aesthetic reward models (ImageReward, HPSv2, LAION aesthetic) that are known to be sensitive to exactly the stylistic descriptors the method amplifies. The descriptor-free and human-study checks help, but the human study is small (15 annotators, 60 pairs), and the appendix is explicitly framed as 'Rebuttal-Driven Additional Experiments', suggesting the evidence was assembled reactively.

Some reported numbers strain plausibility: Table 10 shows identical ~2.11x speedup for skip_ratio from 0.30 to 0.70 even though the spatial path alone contributes 1.43x; and in several qualitative figures (e.g., Fig. 6, Fig. 9) the baseline and AccelAes outputs appear visually identical yet are annotated with different ImageReward values, which undermines confidence in the reported per-image metric gains.

Generality is weaker than claimed: the full spatial SkipSparse path is only deployed on one backbone (Lumina-Next); on SD3 spatial CFG is disabled, and on FLUX the method reduces to temporal caching, where it is actually slower than TeaCache and TaylorSeer. The central 'aesthetic-aware' mechanism is thus validated on essentially one architecture.

The 'training-free' framing obscures meaningful tuning: per-backbone configurations, a hand-curated 34-anchor vocabulary, backbone-specific cache settings, and fallback rules (late-mask, entropy fallback) were developed through pilot tuning and failure mining, which increases overfitting risk to the evaluation prompts.

The appendix retains rebuttal-facing language ('Rebuttal-Driven Additional Experiments') and several references are dated 2026, which is distracting and suggests the manuscript was not carefully revised.

No theoretical or empirical analysis supports the linear-extrapolation cache (Eq. 13) beyond the generic claim that nearby predictions are correlated; error-bounding or trajectory-drift analysis is absent.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core insight: denoising is spatially non-uniform with respect to aesthetic descriptors, and cross-attention provides an internal, training-free signal for allocating compute. This connects inference-time acceleration to perceptual quality in a way that prior uniform caching/token-merging methods do not.

Comprehensive experimental evidence for an applied/algorithmic contribution: three representative DiT backbones (Lumina-Next, SD3-Medium, FLUX.1-dev), a large unified evaluation protocol (10k Pick-a-Pic prompts, fixed seeds, 30k images per configuration, end-to-end latency including VAE and CFG passes), and comparisons against several relevant training-free baselines (∆-DiT, FORA, RAS, SDiT, TeaCache, TaylorSeer).

The ablations are unusually thorough and honest: component-wise decomposition (Table 8/12) shows the spatial path raises ImageReward while temporal caching alone slightly lowers it; the sensitivity studies (skip_ratio, mask_step), static-vs-dynamic mask analysis, failure-case mining with fallback recovery, distilled-model (schnell) compatibility check, and descriptor-free/complex-scene robustness tests all directly probe the plausible objections to the method.

A blind human preference study (15 annotators × 60 pairs, binomial significance tests) validates that the automatic metric gains are not purely artifacts of ImageReward/HPSv2, addressing the most obvious criticism of reward-metric-driven evaluation.

The paper is generally well written and clearly organized; hyperparameters, anchor vocabulary, and per-backbone configurations are documented in sufficient detail to support reproducibility, and code is stated to be available.
Limitations are discussed substantively (dependence on reliable region estimates, diffuse-attention failure cases), which strengthens the scientific case rather than merely decorating it.
weaknesses: The headline claim of simultaneous 2.11× speedup AND improved ImageReward (+11.9%) conflates acceleration with a guidance-strength modification. Spatial-CFG (Eq. 11) effectively raises guidance in focus regions, which is a known lever for improving preference metrics; the dense baseline uses standard uniform CFG. Although the ablation 'w/o Spatial-CFG' and 'w/o AesMask at matched speedup' (0.822 vs 0.841) partially disentangle this, the paper would benefit from a more explicit analysis separating the quality gain due to region-aware guidance from the gain due to compute reallocation, and from comparing against baselines that also tune guidance at matched latency.

Novelty is moderate and mostly combinational: StepCache with linear extrapolation between cached predictions is close to existing forecasting/caching work (FORA, TaylorSeer), and query-sparse attention with global keys/values plus region-adaptive budgets is close to RAS/SDiT. The genuinely new elements are the anchor-based AesMask construction and the coupling of the mask with spatial CFG. The handcrafted 34-anchor vocabulary is a somewhat brittle, prompt-engineering-dependent component, even though the anchor-coverage analysis in Appendix F mitigates this concern.

No confidence intervals or variance reporting for the automatic metrics; some reported gains are small (e.g., CLIP +0.011 on Lumina, HPS +0.003 on FLUX). Given 30k paired images the differences may be reliable, but the paper should state this quantitatively.
The human study is small (15 annotators, 60 pairs) relative to the scale of the automatic evaluation, and alignment vs. the dense baseline is not statistically significant (59%).

Presentation issues reduce polish: Fig. 3 radar plots are qualitative without numbers; the appendix retains rebuttal-internal phrasing ('Rebuttal-Driven Additional Experiments... target three reviewer concerns'), which should be rewritten for a standalone submission; several citations are future-dated or arXiv-only, and the code URL in the abstract is incomplete.

The FLUX configuration uses essentially only the temporal cache (no spatial SkipSparse path), so the strongest claim of the framework (aesthetics-aware spatial allocation) is not validated on one of the three backbones; the FLUX gains therefore largely rest on StepCache, which is the least novel component.

Societal impact is not discussed; while the paper is method-focused, a brief statement on biases inherited from preference/aesthetic reward models (which could skew generation toward certain styles) would be appropriate given that the method explicitly optimizes toward such signals.
